cards.title: Attention is a weighted lookup. Not a dictionary.
cards.body: Queries and keys determine weights; values supply the information being combined. The match is graded, not an exact JSON-key lookup.
cards.detail: Toy example: mixing 25% of 10 with 75% of 30 gives 25. Move the score below and watch the mixture change. Real attention uses vectors.

quiz.question: What does a 25% / 75% mixture of 10 and 30 produce?
quiz.explanation: 0.25 × 10 + 0.75 × 30 = 25. This is a toy scalar calculation, not a trained model.

cards.title: A token is not necessarily a word.
cards.body: Tokenizers turn text into model inputs. Depending on the tokenizer, the pieces can be words, subwords, characters, or bytes.
cards.detail: Try encoding a name, a number and a sentence with an actual tokenizer. Do not estimate the exact token count by counting spaces. Tokenization and the model’s later vector computations are separate steps.

quiz.question: Can you know an exact token count just from the number of words?
options: Yes, one word always equals one token
quiz.explanation: The segmentation depends on the tokenizer and the text.

cards.title: An embedding is a representation—not a definition.
cards.body: An embedding represents an item using a dense vector. Useful relationships can be learned in that space; individual coordinates need not have simple human labels.
cards.detail: Original exercise: imagine three books represented by two numerical features. Which similarities does that representation preserve, and which does it throw away? Real learned embeddings usually have many more dimensions.

cards.title: One prediction becomes the next input.
cards.body: An autoregressive language model generates a continuation by repeatedly predicting the next token from the available prefix.
cards.detail: Original exercise: start with “The door opened and”. Write two different continuations, then extend each again. Early choices alter later context; this does not mean each output was prewritten in a database.

quiz.question: During ordinary autoregressive generation, what happens after a token is selected?
options: It becomes part of the prefix for the next step
quiz.explanation: Generation extends the context; ordinary inference does not retrain the model on each token.

cards.title: Loss tells you what training is rewarding.
cards.body: A loss function measures a particular kind of prediction error. An optimizer changes parameters to reduce that objective—not to satisfy every product goal automatically.
cards.detail: Original exercise: a predictor gets ordinary cases right but misses rare costly failures. Before changing architecture, ask whether your objective and evaluation emphasize the failures you care about.

cards.title: Backpropagation is sensitivity accounting.
cards.body: Automatic differentiation tracks how a computed loss depends on model parameters. Those gradients can guide an optimizer’s updates.
cards.detail: Toy calculation: for L(w) = (w − 3)² at w = 1, the derivative is −4. A gradient-descent step with learning rate 0.1 gives w = 1.4.

quiz.question: What is the update from w = 1 using gradient −4 and rate 0.1?

cards.title: Training changes parameters. Inference uses them.
cards.body: Training fits model parameters to an objective. Inference runs the learned model on an input. Adding context at inference time is not the same operation as retraining.
cards.detail: Original exercise: label three actions—changing a prompt, updating weights from examples, and retrieving a document. Only one necessarily updates model parameters.

quiz.question: Which action necessarily involves a parameter update?
options: Adding a paragraph to the prompt
quiz.explanation: Training updates weights. Prompting and retrieval can operate with fixed weights.

cards.title: The mask prevents a peek at the answer.
cards.body: Causal masking blocks attention to later positions during next-token training.
cards.detail: Original exercise: when predicting C from A B, hide C and everything after it. Parallel training must still respect that boundary.

cards.title: Multiple heads, multiple learned projections.
cards.body: Attention heads use separate learned projections, then combine their outputs.
cards.detail: Do not assign permanent human job titles to each head. “One does grammar” is a teaching guess, not an architectural guarantee.

cards.title: A layer can learn a change, not a replacement.
cards.body: Residual learning adds a learned transformation to an existing representation. The original residual-network research studied much deeper image-recognition networks.
cards.detail: Toy version: y = x + F(x). When F(x) is zero, the block preserves x. That identity path is a different design from requiring every block to reconstruct its input.

quiz.question: For y = x + F(x), what happens when F(x) = 0?

cards.title: Normalization changes scale—not meaning by decree.
cards.body: Layer normalization computes normalization statistics within an individual case rather than across a batch of examples, with learned gain and bias.
cards.detail: Original exercise: compare normalizing one token’s feature vector with normalizing a feature over many training examples. Name the axis before saying “normalize”.

cards.title: Order needs a representation too.
cards.body: The original Transformer adds positional encodings to token embeddings.
cards.detail: Try swapping “dog bites person” to “person bites dog”. The ingredients match; the order changes the relationship.

cards.title: Why stack layers with nonlinearities?
cards.body: Neural networks use hidden layers and activation functions to represent nonlinear relationships. More layers alone are not the complete story.
cards.detail: Toy algebra: composing two affine functions, a(bx + c) + d, still gives an affine function. A nonlinear activation changes the class of functions you can express.

quiz.question: Without nonlinear activations, composing affine layers produces what?
quiz.explanation: Expanding the composition still leaves an affine expression.

cards.title: A perfect training score can be the wrong victory.
cards.body: Overfitting means a model fits its training data in ways that fail to generalize well to new data.
cards.detail: Original exercise: train a small model, then compare training and held-out performance as complexity grows. Keep the test set out of the tuning loop.

cards.title: Pretraining is not the whole assistant.
cards.body: The 2022 InstructGPT study combined supervised demonstrations with preference-based reinforcement learning to improve instruction following.
cards.detail: Treat this as one documented historical recipe, not a description of every later model. Preferred answers can still be wrong; user preference and factual correctness are distinct measurements.

cards.title: Fine-tuning does not always update every weight.
cards.body: LoRA freezes pretrained weights and trains low-rank update matrices. It reduces the number of trainable parameters for an adaptation.
cards.detail: Toy parameter count: a 100 × 100 update has 10,000 entries. Two factors of shapes 100 × 4 and 4 × 100 use 800. This illustrates storage, not a universal accuracy guarantee.

quiz.question: How many entries are in factors shaped 100 × 4 and 4 × 100?

cards.title: Faster attention need not mean approximate attention.
cards.body: FlashAttention reorganizes exact attention around GPU memory access. The engineering improvement is not simply “ignore more token pairs”.
cards.detail: Original exercise: distinguish changing a mathematical operation from executing that operation with less memory traffic. Both can improve speed, but their accuracy implications differ.

cards.title: Fits in context does not mean used reliably.
cards.body: Lost in the Middle found sensitivity to where relevant information appeared in long contexts, on the models and tasks it tested.
cards.detail: Original experiment: put the same answer-bearing paragraph near the start, middle and end of your test inputs. Evaluate your actual model rather than assuming a 2023 result predicts all later systems.

cards.title: Retrieval brings evidence into the workspace.
cards.body: Retrieval-augmented generation combines a language model with retrieved information. The original RAG work coupled parametric memory with a searchable document index.
cards.detail: Original design test: hold the model fixed, change the retrieved passage, and check the answer. Retrieval can supply evidence; it does not automatically make an answer faithful to that evidence.

quiz.question: A retrieved paragraph is irrelevant. Does retrieval alone guarantee a grounded answer?
quiz.explanation: You still need relevant evidence and a check that the answer actually follows it.

cards.title: Not every useful system needs an agent.
cards.body: Anthropic distinguishes predefined workflows from agents that dynamically direct their own process and tool use.
cards.detail: Original design exercise: for a document checker, draw a fixed sequence first. Identify exactly which decision requires flexible model control before introducing a loop with more autonomy.

cards.title: Define success before improving the prompt.
cards.body: An evaluation needs tasks and a way to judge outcomes. An impressive single run is not a substitute for repeatable tests.
cards.detail: Original exercise: write five normal cases, two missing-data cases and two misleading-input cases for a tutor. Keep factual accuracy, helpfulness and tool correctness as separate checks.

cards.title: Your preprocessing can leak the test set.
cards.body: Fitting preprocessing on data that should be held out can leak information into training. Pipelines help keep fitting inside the appropriate training split.
cards.detail: Original exercise: split first, fit the scaler on training data, then transform validation data with the fitted scaler. Ask the same question about feature selection and imputation.

quiz.question: Where should a scaler be fitted for a held-out evaluation?
quiz.explanation: Fit learned preprocessing only on the training split, then apply it to held-out data.

cards.title: Accuracy can hide the mistake you care about.
cards.body: Precision asks how many predicted positives were positive. Recall asks how many actual positives were found. They answer different questions.
cards.detail: Toy case: flag 10 items, 8 truly positive, out of 20 actual positives. Precision is 8/10 = 80%; recall is 8/20 = 40%.

quiz.question: In that example, what is recall?

cards.title: Saved on this device is not an account.
cards.body: Browser localStorage can persist between visits, but it belongs to an origin and browser profile. It is not cross-device synchronization or a protected user database.
cards.detail: For this feed: saved cards and practice attempts stay in this browser. Export creates a file you control. Clearing site data removes the local copy. A same-origin script can access localStorage.

cards.title: A KV cache is computation reuse, not life memory.
cards.body: During generation, a KV cache reuses previously computed keys and values. This saves repeated work but consumes memory.
cards.detail: Original exercise: distinguish a generation cache from a database of user preferences. They may both be called “memory”, but they have different lifetimes and purposes.

cards.title: Retrieved text is data—not authority.
cards.body: Prompt injection can hide instructions inside content a system processes. A document’s instruction to take an action should not acquire the application’s permissions.
cards.detail: Original design exercise: give a summarizer an untrusted paragraph asking it to disclose private data. Keep access controls and action approval outside the text being summarized.

cards.title: The cost is the best alternative you give up.
cards.body: Opportunity cost concerns the value of the next-best forgone alternative—not the sum of every possible alternative.
cards.detail: Original scenario: you can spend one evening coding, reading or going out. To compare coding with its opportunity cost, identify the best of the alternatives you would otherwise choose.

quiz.question: Which alternative defines opportunity cost?
quiz.explanation: Opportunity cost uses the next-best alternative, not every alternative combined.

cards.title: An equilibrium is a model condition, not a promise.
cards.body: In a competitive supply-and-demand model, a market-clearing price balances quantity demanded and quantity supplied.
cards.detail: Toy market: demand = 100 − 2p and supply = 20 + 2p. Setting them equal gives p = 20 and quantity = 60. Real markets require additional assumptions and evidence.

quiz.question: For those toy curves, what is the clearing price?

cards.title: A model is useful partly because it leaves things out.
cards.body: Economic models isolate mechanisms through explicit simplifications. The assumptions define where a result may travel—and where it may not.
cards.detail: Original exercise: take the toy market on the previous card. Add a capacity limit, delayed production, or a dominant seller. Which result must you now recheck? This is a modeling exercise, not investment advice.

cards.title: What did you observe? What did you infer?
cards.body: The Library of Congress encourages observing a source, reflecting on it and asking further questions. Keep those steps distinct.
cards.detail: Original exercise: a diary says, “We departed before dawn.” That supports a departure claim. It does not, by itself, establish the writer’s motive. Put the motive in an inference column and seek another source.

quiz.question: A diary records departure before dawn. Which claim requires more evidence?
options: The diary reports an early departure
The writer departed because of fear
quiz.explanation: The stated time and an inferred motive are different kinds of claims.

cards.title: Pause the story before you know the ending.
cards.body: South is Shackleton’s account of his expedition. Use it as a source to question, not only as a story to admire.
cards.detail: Original reading exercise: stop at a decision point. Write the options, available information and uncertainties before reading on. Then compare your reasoning with the account. This exercise is not a quotation or a claim about a particular decision.

cards.title: Recognizing an explanation is not recalling it.
cards.body: Roediger and Karpicke found benefits of retrieval practice for delayed retention in their prose-learning experiments. That is not evidence that scrolling alone creates mastery.
cards.detail: Original exercise: close one expanded card and explain its idea without looking. Then reopen it and check one omission. This feed records an attempted question separately from a viewed card.

cards.title: A compact map of machine learning
cards.body: Burkov’s book introduces a range of ML methods, their mathematics and practical considerations.
cards.detail: Our reading task: choose one unfamiliar term and pair it with one tiny implementation. This is an entry point based on the author’s description, not a chapter summary.

cards.title: Build the pieces instead of only calling the API
cards.body: Raschka’s book walks through constructing a GPT-style language model, including training and adaptation.
cards.detail: Our reading task: inspect tensor shapes and write a test for one component before moving to the next. The publisher page includes sample and code links.

cards.title: From a foundation model to an application
cards.body: Chip Huyen’s AI Engineering focuses on applications built with available foundation models.
cards.detail: Our reading task: choose a product workflow, then write down its inputs, evaluation criteria and failure behavior. This card describes the book’s scope, not its full contents.

cards.title: The model lives inside a larger system
cards.body: Designing Machine Learning Systems is a separate Chip Huyen book focused on ML systems.
cards.detail: Our reading task: list the data, deployment, monitoring and feedback components around a model you understand. Use the author’s page to reach the book.

cards.title: Keep a foundations reference nearby
cards.body: Deep Learning, by Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, provides an author-hosted online text, from mathematical foundations to neural-network methods.
cards.detail: Our reading task: use its table of contents to resolve one prerequisite rather than trying to read every chapter at once.

cards.title: Watch a learning engine take shape
cards.body: Karpathy’s micrograd lecture builds automatic differentiation and a small neural network from scratch.
cards.detail: Our viewing task: pause before a derivative is computed and predict its sign. Video loads only after you choose to connect to YouTube.

cards.title: Turn the Transformer paper into code
cards.body: Karpathy’s GPT lecture constructs a small autoregressive Transformer language model.
cards.detail: Our viewing task: identify the token inputs, causal mask and next-token loss. The author’s syllabus links the prerequisite lessons.

cards.title: Build the step before the neural network
cards.body: Karpathy’s tokenizer lecture explores text encoding and byte-pair encoding through implementation.
cards.detail: Our viewing task: compare two strings that look similar to a reader but may segment differently. No transcript is republished here.

cards.title: Return to the original architecture
cards.body: A reference route into the 2017 Transformer paper.
cards.detail: Reading task: follow one input through section 3. Separate the historical architecture from later variants.

cards.title: Read the original retrieval-augmented formulation
cards.body: The RAG paper joins learned model parameters with an external retrieval index.
cards.detail: Our reading task: distinguish this paper’s specific model from the broad family of systems now described as retrieval-augmented.

cards.title: Inspect a smaller trainable update
cards.body: The LoRA paper describes low-rank adaptation of pretrained models.
cards.detail: Our reading task: identify what remains frozen, what is learned and which reported result depends on an experimental setup.

cards.title: An algorithm can improve the memory path
cards.body: FlashAttention is a reference on IO-aware exact attention.
cards.detail: Our reading task: separate mathematical equivalence from measured runtime. Hardware and implementation affect the latter.

cards.title: A historical route from prediction to instruction following
cards.body: The InstructGPT paper documents a particular human-feedback training method.
cards.detail: Our reading task: distinguish demonstrations, preference comparisons and model evaluation. Avoid treating one study as every assistant’s recipe.

cards.title: Test the position of your evidence
cards.body: Lost in the Middle investigates how long-context performance depends on relevant information placement.
cards.detail: Our reading task: note the tested tasks and models before generalizing. Design your own controlled placement test.

cards.title: Find a connection between vision and language models
cards.body: Residual learning was studied in deep image-recognition networks.
cards.detail: Our reading task: separate the reusable residual idea from the original paper’s computer-vision results.

cards.title: Name the normalization axis
cards.body: Layer Normalization contrasts within-case normalization with batch-dependent normalization.
cards.detail: Our reading task: sketch which values contribute to a mean and variance in each method.

cards.title: Use the tokenizer lesson as a debugging reference
cards.body: Hugging Face’s lesson explains tokenization approaches and encoding.
cards.detail: Our reading task: test actual encode/decode behavior rather than inferring token boundaries from typography.

cards.title: Trace a real gradient computation
cards.body: PyTorch’s autograd tutorial shows automatic differentiation in a computational graph.
cards.detail: Our build task: change one input and check the resulting gradient. Consult the documentation version matching your installed package.

cards.title: Inspect a complete training loop
cards.body: The PyTorch optimization tutorial connects a loss, backward pass and optimizer step.
cards.detail: Our build task: name what changes after each step and what must be reset before the next iteration.

cards.title: Audit an experiment before believing its score
cards.body: scikit-learn’s pitfalls guide covers mistakes such as leaking held-out information into training.
cards.detail: Our review task: trace every fit operation back to the rows it could see.

cards.title: Choose the question your metric answers
cards.body: scikit-learn documents prediction metrics and scoring conventions.
cards.detail: Our build task: calculate precision and recall by hand for a tiny confusion matrix, then compare with code.

cards.title: Begin with the simplest sufficient workflow
cards.body: Anthropic’s guide distinguishes workflow patterns and agentic control.
cards.detail: Our design task: mark which steps require judgment and which should stay deterministic.

cards.title: Evaluate an outcome, not just impressive prose
cards.body: Anthropic’s evaluation article discusses tasks, trials and graders for agents.
cards.detail: Our build task: write a failing case before improving the system. Keep evidence of task completion separate from the explanation.

cards.title: Make the trust boundary visible
cards.body: OWASP’s prompt-injection entry explains risks when model inputs contain hostile instructions.
cards.detail: Our design task: separate text processing from permissions to read private data or execute actions.

cards.title: Read an expedition through its own account
cards.body: South offers Shackleton’s written account, available in a public-domain US edition.
cards.detail: Our reading task: compare the narrator’s explanation with the evidence available at the time. Distinguish the account from a later historical synthesis.

cards.title: A method for reading evidence
cards.body: The Library of Congress offers guidance for analyzing primary sources.
cards.detail: Our reading task: keep three columns—observation, interpretation and unanswered question. Apply the method to a letter, photograph or newspaper page.

cards.title: A useful interface tells you what just happened
cards.body: Nielsen’s usability heuristics emphasize visible status, user control and error prevention.
cards.detail: Our design exercise: imagine saving a card with no feedback. What would reassure you without blocking your next action?

cards.title: Ask what an explanation actually explains
cards.body: Molnar’s Interpretable Machine Learning is an author-hosted reference on interpreting models.
cards.detail: Our reading task: distinguish an explanation of a prediction from proof that the prediction is correct. Start with the book’s introduction.

paths.title: Inside a Transformer
paths.description: From token pieces to representations, attention and generation. An editorial sequence, not a mastery test.

paths.title: Build a reliable AI workflow
paths.description: Define success, select evidence, control actions and evaluate what actually happened.

paths.title: Evidence, models & decisions
paths.description: Practice distinguishing observation, assumption and a conclusion that still needs testing.
